summary: Describes measures to make DNS resolvers much harder to fool with forged answers, such as behavior that had not previously been standardized. It addresses a serious threat while DNS security was not yet fully deployed. This is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2181.

eli5.summary: Someone might sneak a fake answer into the Internet phone book. This memo lists ways for the lookup helper to spot and throw away fakes.

questions: how hard is it to forge a dns answer
what must a dns resolver check in a response
subtitle: Rules that make a caching DNS resolver far harder to fool with fake answers, without changing the DNS protocol.

tldr.problem: A caching resolver accepts the first reply that matches a handful of fields, and attackers can guess those fields. A forged answer is then cached and handed to every client.
tldr.mechanism: Resolvers must match replies on address, port, query ID, name, class and type, and must use unpredictable source ports and query IDs so the guessing space grows far beyond 16 bits.
tldr.outcome: A resolver following these rules makes forgery orders of magnitude harder. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2181 and is meant to hold until cryptographic DNS security is deployed.

today: RFC 5452 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2009. It updates RFC 2181 and, according to the metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why Forged Answers Matter
sections.content:
Almost every transaction on the Internet uses the Domain Name System. Whoever controls DNS even briefly can reroute most kinds of traffic. The RFC points out that it had become possible to get an SSL/TLS certificate by answering a verification email, and email routing generally uses DNS. So even traffic protected by SSL/TLS could be diverted.

The goal is to make the existing DNS as secure as possible within the current protocol boundaries, until a cryptographically enhanced DNS is finalized and deployed. The RFC says the most commonly used resolvers did not perform as well as possible, which made it urgent. Even a cryptographically secured DNS benefits from discarding bogus responses quickly, because that saves computation.

Even with every measure applied, users are not protected against third parties who can observe, modify or inject packets in a resolver's traffic. For that, the RFC points to DNSSEC (RFC 4033 and beyond).
sections.eli5: If someone tricks the phone book, every call goes to the wrong person. This memo is about making the phone book harder to trick.

sections.title: What Makes a Resolver Accept an Answer
sections.content:
A resolver is a nameserver that does recursive work for clients and caches what it learns. Once it is spoofed, the RFC notes, a caching server repeats the wrongly accepted data and makes its clients contact the wrong, possibly malicious, servers.

DNS data is accepted if and only if four conditions hold:

  • the question section of the reply is equivalent to that of a question packet waiting for a response;
  • the ID field of the reply matches that of the question;
  • the reply comes from the same network address the question was sent to;
  • the reply arrives at the same address, including port number, the question was sent from.

In general the first response matching these conditions is accepted. An attacker who meets them before the authentic server answers can feed the resolver fabricated data.
sections.eli5: The librarian only checks that the note has the right title, the right secret number, the right sender and the right door. If a fake note gets all four right first, the librarian believes it.

sections.title: How an Attacker Guesses Each Piece
sections.content:
Forcing a query. Attackers need the resolver to ask the question. An open recursive server lets them ask directly; otherwise they can induce a mail server to do lookups. Resolvers also publish the decreasing time to live (TTL) of cached entries, which shows when a refresh query will happen. A short TTL means more windows of opportunity.

The ID field. It is 16 bits wide, so truly random use takes on average 32768 guesses. The RFC mentions anecdotal evidence of implementations using only 14 bits, which needs on average 8192 attempts.

Addresses. Spoofing the authoritative server's source address needs no more than two or three attempts for a zone with two or three nameservers, and ingress filtering (RFC 2827) was not widely implemented.

Port. Most resolvers then picked one port at startup, and often it was fixed at 53. Any authoritative server the attacker watches reveals that port, so matching it needs no guessing. A random port per query acts as a second ID of up to 16 bits.

Timing. Once a packet matches, later responses are generally rejected. The RFC assumes a window of at most 100 ms, which can be longer if authoritative servers are overloaded.
sections.eli5: The faker has to guess a secret number, which door to use and who the sender is. Some of those are easy to learn, so the hard part is the secret number and the door.

sections.title: Birthday Attacks and In-Domain Records
sections.content:
The birthday paradox says 23 people are enough for a better than even chance that two share a birthday. If an attacker can force a resolver to have several identical outstanding queries (same QNAME, QTYPE and QCLASS) to the same server, one fake packet only has to match any one of them. For small numbers of queries the chance of success rises linearly with the number of outstanding queries.

Responses also carry extra data outside the queried zone, for example the address of a mail exchanger in another domain. Accepting it uncritically means trusting an untrusted source. A resolver must only accept data when the originator is known to be authoritative for the QNAME or a parent of it. A very simple way is to accept only data that is part of the domain the query was for.
sections.eli5: If the librarian has many identical questions waiting, a fake note has more chances to match one. And the librarian should ignore side notes about things the sender has no business talking about.

sections.title: How Hard Is a Forgery, in Numbers
sections.content:
The RFC gives a probability formula: with D identical outstanding queries, F fake packets, N authoritative servers, P ports and I IDs, the chance of being spoofed in one window is D * F / (N * P * I). A new window opens each time the TTL expires, so over a time T there are T / TTL attempts.

With a known or static port, matching the ID and both addresses takes on average about 65000 packets for a zone with 2 nameservers. In a 100 ms window that means sending 650000 packets per second for a 50% chance on the first attempt, roughly 416 Mbit/s for 80-byte packets. If the window is stretched to a second the figure falls to 42 Mbit/s. With 60 minutes of attempts against a domain with a 300 second TTL, 4 Mbit/s suffices.

Example: against a record with a 3600 second TTL, 7000 fake packets per second (4.5 Mbit/s) gives a 10% chance within 24 hours and 50% after a week. If the port also has to be guessed, the problem space grows by a factor of 64000 and the attacker would need in excess of 285 Gb/s. Where techniques reduce the effective TTL to 0, one source port gives a 50% chance within 7 seconds, while 64000 ports push the 50% level to around 116 hours.
sections.eli5: With a fixed door, a determined faker gets lucky fairly soon. When the door changes randomly every time, luck takes thousands of hours.

sections.title: The Countermeasures
sections.content:
A resolver MUST match a response against all of these attributes of the query before applying the DNS trustworthiness rules of RFC 2181: source address against query destination address, destination address against query source address, destination port against query source port, query ID, query name, and query class and type. Any mismatch makes the response invalid.

To enlarge the guessing space, resolvers MUST use an unpredictable source port for outgoing queries from the largest practicable range (53, or 1024 and above), use several different source ports at once when queries are outstanding, and use an unpredictable query ID over the full range 0-65535. Resolvers with multiple IP addresses SHOULD use them unpredictably, and SHOULD let operators avoid certain ports.

Resolvers SHOULD favor authoritative servers they have a trust relation with, and stub resolvers SHOULD be able to use TSIG (RFC 2845) or IPsec toward their recursive resolver. Where TSIG or SIG(0) verification is available, a resolver MAY waive the rules above. Good unpredictability needs a high quality random generator as described in RFC 4086.

If a resolver detects a spoofing attempt, for example many packets failing the checks, it MAY abandon the UDP query and retry over TCP, which resists forgery far better because of its sequence numbers.
sections.eli5: The librarian now checks every detail, picks secret numbers and doors that nobody can predict, and if a prankster seems to be around, switches to a safer way of talking.

sections.title: Security and NAT Side Effects
sections.content:
The RFC says its recommendations complement later cryptographic enhancements of DNS, which protect against a larger class of attacks. A resolver that ignores them can easily be forced to accept spoofed responses and misdirect client traffic.

Source port randomization can be dramatically weakened by NAT devices that serialize or limit the UDP source ports a resolver uses. Randomization also makes NAT or stateful firewall entries get consumed faster. The RFC suggests such boxes purge outgoing DNS query translation entries 10-17 seconds after the last outgoing query on that mapping, and that services which generate many DNS queries per connection, especially email servers, be rate limited. Some firewalls may need reconfiguring if they only allow queries from a single source port.
sections.eli5: Some doormen at the building always send you out the same door, which spoils the trick. And using many doors keeps the doormen busy, so they should tidy up quickly.
